timeline.text: The adult human skull has twenty-two bones: eight cranial bones enclose the brain, and fourteen facial bones form the face.
Frontal bone. It forms the forehead and brow ridges, and much of the anterior cranial fossa and orbital roofs.
Parietal bones, left and right. Together they form the roof and much of the side walls of the cranium.
Temporal bones, left and right. Their petrous parts contain the inner ear, with organs of hearing and balance.
Occipital bone. It forms the back and part of the base of the cranium. At the foramen magnum, the medulla continues as the spinal cord.
Sphenoid bone. Shaped like a butterfly, it sits centrally in the cranial base and contributes to both orbits.
Ethmoid bone. Light and delicate, it lies between the two orbits. It forms parts of the nasal cavity and the medial orbital walls.
Nasal bones, left and right. Together they form the bony bridge of the nose.
Lacrimal bones, left and right, are small bones in the medial orbital walls. They contribute to the fossa for the lacrimal sac.
Maxillae, left and right, form much of the upper jaw. They hold the upper teeth and contain the maxillary sinuses.
Zygomatic bones, left and right, form the cheek prominences. They also contribute to the orbital walls and zygomatic arches.
Palatine bones, left and right, form the posterior hard palate. They also contribute to the nasal cavity and a small part of each orbit.
Inferior nasal conchae, left and right, are scroll-shaped bones on the lateral nasal walls. Their mucosal covering helps warm and humidify inspired air.
Vomer. A single midline bone, it forms the posteroinferior part of the bony nasal septum.
Mandible. The largest and strongest facial bone, it moves at the temporomandibular joints during chewing and speech.
Separated, all twenty-two bones are shown in this teaching model.
And back together: a complete bony skull.
Apart, the individual bones are easier to identify. Together, they protect the brain and support the face.
